stories.title: LHAASO detection of ultrahigh-energy γ-ray emission towards giant molecular clouds
stories.description: γ-ray emission from giant molecular clouds (GMCs) is regarded as the most ideal tool to perform in situ measurement of cosmic ray (CR) density and spectra in our Galaxy. Here we report a detection of very-high-energy γ-ray emission from five nearby GMCs using a stacking analysis of 4.5 years of observations with the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). The spectral energy distributions derived for the GMCs are consistent with the expected γ-ray flux produced via CRs interacting with the interstellar medium over 1–100 TeV. We also search for the CR spectral ‘knee’ by introducing a break into the γ-ray model. Although no clear knee signature is detected, current KM2A measurements of the GMCs are broadly compatible with a proton CR knee around or above 0.9 PeV, although somewhat lower break energies cannot be excluded within the current uncertainties. This result is broadly consistent with recent ground-based CR measurements. Ultimately, the detection of very-high-energy γ-ray emission from GMCs establishes these regions as crucial laboratories for mapping the spatial distribution of CRs across the Milky Way, offering a unique avenue to fundamentally advancing our understanding of the origin and propagation of galactic CRs. LHAASO observations reveal ultrahigh-energy γ-rays from nearby giant molecular clouds, identifying these clouds as natural laboratories for mapping cosmic rays across the Milky Way.

stories.title: Music therapy and Alzheimer’s: finding connection when memories fade
stories.description: September is World Alzheimer’s Month, a time to raise awareness about Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia and to challenge the stigma surrounding them. For people living with dementia, as well as their families and caregivers, the effects can be profound. Memory loss is perhaps the symptom most commonly associated with Alzheimer’s, but the disease can also involve anxiety, isolation, loss of independence and a gradual disconnection from the people and world around us. Among the approaches used to support people living with dementia, music therapy offers a particularly intriguing possibility. People forget things, their daily lives, they forget people's names, this kind of thing. And that is certainly a part of it.” In his work, however, the challenges extend well beyond forgetting names or everyday information. Klassen estimates that approximately 80 percent of his work week is spent with people living with Alzheimer’s and related dementias, giving him a close-up view of the cumulative effects of the disease. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/chv_ros_bb', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1616015438375-bbm3'); s.setConfig({targeting: {URL: [window.location.pathname]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {position: [1616015438375]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {story_id: 'music-therapy-and-alzheimers-finding-connection-when-memories-fade'}}) s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); “Some of the most challenging things about it are the anxiety that can build up, the loss of self. And really there's a series of losses that this person is going through. They're losing connection to others. They've lost their livelihood, potentially. They've lost their driver's license. There's a lot of loss. They're losing their independence bit by bit.” It is this accumulation of losses that often becomes the focus of his therapeutic work. Music, rather than simply being entertainment, becomes a means of helping people reconnect with themselves and with those around them. The micro-miracles of music Videos showing people with advanced dementia suddenly responding to familiar music can be remarkably moving. Someone who appears withdrawn may begin singing, tapping their feet or engaging with the people around them after hearing a song from their past. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/chv_ros_bb', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1616015438375-bbm4'); s.setConfig({targeting: {URL: [window.location.pathname]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {position: [1616015438375]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {story_id: 'music-therapy-and-alzheimers-finding-connection-when-memories-fade'}}) s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); Klassen says these dramatic examples represent an extreme version of something he sees regularly. “Well, In a way, yes. Simply playing a recording does not necessarily produce the same therapeutic result as working with someone in a structured, personal setting. “It's almost every day I work with smaller micro miracles with people in relation to music.” Why music can reach so deeply One of the most fascinating questions surrounding music and dementia is why musical memories can sometimes remain accessible when other memories appear to have disappeared. googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/chv_ros_bb', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1616015438375-bbm5'); s.setConfig({targeting: {URL: [window.location.pathname]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {position: [1616015438375]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {story_id: 'music-therapy-and-alzheimers-finding-connection-when-memories-fade'}}) s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); Klassen describes a common example: a person may struggle to remember their own name but suddenly sing an entire song from decades earlier. “People will say this over and over. You know, my mom can't even remember her first name anymore. But then you put on this song and she sings all the words word for word.” Modern brain-imaging technology is helping researchers better understand why this can happen. Klassen points to functional MRI research showing that music activates numerous areas of the brain rather than being confined to one isolated “music centre.” “Now we can see that most of the brain is lit up by music. It's not that we have this music center in our brain and my music center is bigger than yours or whatever. It's that the speech center, the movement center, the social connections center, the memory center, the motor receptor, the mirror neurons that help someone feel like they're playing the guitar just by watching someone else play guitar. All of these centers are lit up by music.” googletag.cmd.push(function() { if($(document).width()<900) { s = googletag.defineSlot('/50748803/chv_ros_bb', [300, 250], 'div-gpt-1616015438375-bbm6'); s.setConfig({targeting: {URL: [window.location.pathname]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {position: [1616015438375]}}) s.setConfig({targeting: {story_id: 'music-therapy-and-alzheimers-finding-connection-when-memories-fade'}}) s.addService(googletag.pubads()); googletag.pubads().refresh([s], {changeCorrelator: false}); } }); That broad neurological engagement may help explain why music can sometimes provide alternative pathways for communication and expression. Klassen points to the well-known case of former U.S. congresswoman Gabby Giffords, who experienced a severe brain injury from a gunshot. A music therapist worked with her using singing as a way to help her communicate. “One of the most helpful things they did together was that she sang whatever she wanted to speak. And she was able to sing the very same words that were blocked by her injury.” He describes music as finding a way around the damaged area of the brain, while acknowledging that this is an oversimplification of a complicated neurological process. And I'm dragging a suitcase full of drums and shakers and all kinds of random things. And really I'm there to motivate them to make music with me, with each other.” That active participation is central to the therapeutic relationship. Rather than treating music as the end result, he uses it as a tool for creating interaction. “And it's in the making of music that relationship is formed, the therapeutic relationship that can tap into who I am as a person, relating with who they are as a person. And the music is really just the tool to make that happen.” Consistency is another important element. For people living with dementia, a predictable structure can provide a sense of familiarity and safety. Relatives often know the musical history of a person in a way that a therapist meeting them for the first time cannot. Their observations can help identify significant responses to particular songs. stories.title: These massive stars could explain Webb’s strangest galaxies
stories.description: Hubble observations of massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies are revealing clues to why the early universe looks so unusual. Researchers found that stellar winds weaken sharply at extremely low metallicities, potentially allowing massive stars to retain more material and evolve in unexpected ways. The team also found large differences in iron abundance, a key ingredient in stellar winds and supernovae.
